peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
When I examine myself, Seneca, some vices appear on the surface,
and so that I can lay my hands upon them, while others are less
distinct and harder to reach, and some are not always present, but
recur at intervals: and these I should call the most troublesome,
being like a roving enemy that assails one when he sees his
opportunity, and who will neither let one stand on one’s guard as
in war, nor yet take one’s rest without fear as in peace. The
position in which I find myself more especially (for why should I
not tell you the truth as I would to a physician), is that of neither
being thoroughly set free from the vices which I fear and hate, nor
yet quite in bondage to them: my state of mind, though not the worst
possible, is a particularly discontented and sulky one: I am neither
ill nor well, It is of no use for you to tell me that all virtues
are weakly at the outset, and that they acquire strength and solidity
by time, for I am well aware that even those which do but help our
outward show, such as grandeur, a reputation for eloquence, and
everything that appeals to others, gain power by time.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: When I look at myself, Serenus, some of my flaws are right on the surface where I can grab them. Others are harder to see and reach. Some don't stick around all the time — they come and go. These are the worst kind. They're like guerrilla fighters who attack when they see a chance, then disappear. You can't stay on guard like in war, but you can't relax like in peacetime either. Here's my real situation (why shouldn't I tell you the truth, like I would a doctor): I'm not completely free from the vices I fear and hate, but I'm not totally enslaved by them either. My state of mind isn't the worst possible, but it's particularly restless and grumpy. I'm neither sick nor healthy. Don't bother telling me that all virtues start weak and get stronger over time — I already know that. Even things that just improve our image, like impressive speaking or reputation, grow stronger with practice.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
Both those
which afford us real strength and those which do but trick
us out in a more attractive form, require long years before they
gradually are adapted to us by time. But I fear that custom, which
confirms most things, implants this vice more and more deeply in
me. Long acquaintance with both good and bad people leads one to
esteem them all alike. What this state of weakness really is, when
the mind halts between two opinions without any strong inclination
towards either good or evil, I shall be better able to show you
piecemeal than all at once. I will tell you what befalls me, you
must find out the name of the disease. I have to confess the greatest
possible love of thrift: I do not care for a bed with gorgeous
hangings, nor for clothes brought out of a chest, or pressed under
weights and made glossy by frequent manglings, but for common and
cheap ones, that require no care either to keep them or to put them
on.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: The habits that actually make us stronger and the ones that just make us look good both take years to stick. Time slowly shapes us to fit them. But I worry that this same process is making my problem worse. The longer I know both good and bad people, the more I treat them all the same. This weakness I'm talking about — when your mind gets stuck between two choices without really wanting either the good or the bad — I can show you better through examples than by explaining it all at once. I'll tell you what happens to me. You can figure out what to call this condition.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
For food I do not want what needs whole troops of servants to
prepare it and admire it, nor what is ordered many days before and
served up by many hands, but something handy and easily come at,
with nothing far-fetched or costly about it, to be had in every
part of the world, burdensome neither to one’s fortune nor one’s
body, not likely to go out of the body by the same path by which
it came in. I like[1] a rough and unpolished homebred servant, I
like my servant born in my house: I like my country-bred father’s
heavy silver plate stamped with no maker’s name: I do not want a
table that is beauteous with dappled spots, or known to all the
town by the number of fashionable people to whom it has successively
belonged, but one which stands merely for use, and which causes no
guest’s eye to dwell upon it with pleasure or to kindle at it with
envy. While I am well satisfied with this, I am reminded of the
clothes of a certain schoolboy, dressed with no ordinary care and
splendour, of slaves bedecked with gold and a whole regiment
of glittering attendants.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I have to admit I love living simply. I don't want a bed with fancy decorations or clothes that come from expensive chests — clothes that need to be pressed and polished until they shine. I prefer ordinary, cheap clothes that don't need special care when I store them or put them on. For food, I don't want meals that need armies of servants to prepare and present, or dishes that must be ordered days ahead and handled by many people. I want something simple and easy to get. Nothing exotic or expensive. Food you can find anywhere in the world, that won't hurt your wallet or your body, and that won't make you sick later. I like a rough, unrefined servant who was born and raised at home. I like my father's heavy silver — the plain country kind with no fancy maker's mark. I don't want a table that's beautiful with elegant patterns, or one that's famous around town because so many fashionable people have owned it. I want a table that's just useful — one that doesn't make guests stare at it in wonder or burn with envy.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
I think of houses too, where one treads
on precious stones, and where valuables lie about in every corner,
where the very roof is brilliantly painted, and a whole nation
attends and accompanies an inheritance on the road to ruin. What
shall I say of waters, transparent to the very bottom, which flow
round the guests, and banquets worthy of the theatre in which they
take place? Coming as I do from a long course of dull thrift, I
find myself surrounded by the most brilliant luxury, which echoes
around me on every side: my sight becomes a little dazzled by it:
I can lift up my heart against it more easily than my eyes. When I
return from seeing it I am a sadder, though not a worse man, I
cannot walk amid my own paltry possessions with so lofty a step as
before, and silently there steals over me a feeling of vexation,
and a doubt whether that way of life may not be better than mine.
None of these things alter my principles, yet all of them disturb
me.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: While I'm content with my simple life, I can't help but think about certain extravagant scenes I've witnessed. A schoolboy dressed in incredibly fine clothes. Slaves covered in gold jewelry and a whole parade of glittering servants. Houses where you walk on precious stones and valuables are scattered in every corner. Ceilings painted with brilliant colors. An entire nation following some inheritance down the path to bankruptcy. What about those crystal-clear pools that flow around dinner guests? And banquets so elaborate they belong in a theater? Coming from my plain, careful lifestyle, I suddenly find myself surrounded by the most dazzling luxury. It echoes around me from every direction. My eyes get overwhelmed by it all. I can steel my heart against it more easily than I can control what I'm seeing. When I come home from these scenes, I'm sadder — though not a worse person. I can't walk through my own humble belongings with the same confident stride as before. A quiet irritation creeps over me, along with doubt about whether their way of life might actually be better than mine. None of these experiences change my principles, but all of them shake me up.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
At one time I would obey the maxims of our school and plunge
into public life, I would obtain office and become consul, not
because the purple robe and lictor’s axes attract me, but in order
that I may be able to be of use to my friends, my relatives, to all
my countrymen, and indeed to all mankind. Ready and determined, I
follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus, all of whom
bid one take part in public affairs, though none of them ever did
so himself: and then, as soon as something disturbs my mind, which
is not used to receiving shocks, as soon as something occurs which
is either disgraceful, such as often occurs in all men’s lives, or
which does not proceed quite easily, or when subjects of very little
importance require me to devote a great deal of time to them, I go
back to my life of leisure, and, just as even tired cattle go faster
when they are going home, I wish to retire and pass my life within
the walls of my house. “No one,” I say, “that will give me no
compensation worth such a loss shall ever rob me of a day.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: Sometimes I follow our school's teachings and throw myself into public life. I seek office and aim to become consul — not because I want the purple robe or the ceremonial axes, but because I want to help my friends, my family, my fellow citizens, and all humanity. Ready and determined, I follow the advice of Zeno, Cleanthes, and Chrysippus. They all tell us to participate in public affairs, though none of them actually did it themselves. But then something upsets my mind, which isn't used to being shocked. Something disgraceful happens (as it often does in everyone's life), or things don't go smoothly, or trivial matters demand huge amounts of my time. So I retreat back to my private life. Like tired cattle walking faster when they're heading home, I want to retire and live within the walls of my house. "No one," I tell myself, "will rob me of even a day unless they can pay me back with something worthwhile. Let my mind focus on itself and improve itself. Let it stay out of other people's business and do nothing that depends on others' approval. Let me enjoy peace that's undisturbed by either public or private troubles."

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
Write something therefore in
a simple style, merely to pass the time, for your own use, and not
for publication. Less labour is needed when one does not look beyond
the present.” Then again, when the mind is elevated by the greatness
of its thoughts, it becomes ostentatious in its use of words, the
loftier its aspirations, the more loftily it desires to express
them, and its speech rises to the dignity of its subject. At such
times I forget my mild and moderate determination and soar higher
than is my wont, using a language that is not my own. Not to multiply
examples, I am in all things attended by this weakness of a
well-meaning mind, to whose level I fear that I shall be gradually
brought down, or, what is even more worrying, that I may always
hang as though about to fall, and that there may be more the matter
with me than I myself perceive: for we take a friendly view of our
own private affairs, and partiality always obscures our judgment.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I won't pile on more examples. But I struggle with this weakness in everything I do — I have good intentions, but I'm shaky about following through. I'm afraid I'll gradually sink to a lower level. Or worse, I'll always be hanging there like I'm about to fall. And there might be more wrong with me than I even realize. We see our own problems through rose-colored glasses. Our bias always clouds our judgment. I think many people could have reached wisdom if they hadn't convinced themselves they were already there. They lie to themselves about parts of their character and deliberately ignore other parts. You have no reason to think other people's flattery hurts us more than our own. Who has the guts to tell himself the truth? Who isn't his own biggest flatterer, even when surrounded by a crowd of sweet-talking admirers? So please — if you have any cure that could stop this back-and-forth in my mind, help me. Let me owe my peace of mind to you. I know these mental swings aren't dangerous. They don't threaten me with any serious illness. To put it exactly: I'm not caught in a storm, just seasick. Take this problem away from me, whatever it is. Help someone who's struggling in sight of shore.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
I fancy that many men would have arrived at wisdom had they
not believed themselves to have arrived there already, had they not
purposely deceived themselves as to some parts of their character,
and passed by others with their eyes shut: for you have no grounds
for supposing that other people’s flattery is more ruinous to us
than our own. Who dares to tell himself the truth? Who is there,
by however large a troop of caressing courtiers he may be surrounded,
who in spite of them is not his own greatest flatterer? I beg you,
therefore, if you have any remedy by which you could stop this
vacillation of mine, to deem me worthy to owe my peace of mind to
you. I am well aware that these oscillations of mind are not perilous
and that they threaten me with no serious disorder: to express what
I complain of by an exact simile, I am not suffering from a storm,
but from sea-sickness. Take from me, then, this evil, whatever it
may be, and help one who is in distress within sight of land.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I think many people would have found wisdom if they hadn't already convinced themselves they were wise. They lie to themselves about parts of their character and ignore other parts completely. Don't think that other people's flattery hurts us more than our own. Who dares to tell themselves the truth? Even someone surrounded by a crowd of fawning courtiers — who is still their own worst flatterer? So please, if you have any cure that could stop this wavering of mine, help me find peace of mind. I know these mental swings aren't dangerous. They won't cause serious harm. To put it exactly: I'm not caught in a storm, but I am seasick. Take away this problem, whatever it is, and help someone who's struggling within sight of shore.

peace-of-mind_section-01.originalText:
Let my mind be contained within itself and improve itself: let it
take no part with other men’s affairs, and do nothing which depends
on the approval of others: let me enjoy a tranquillity undisturbed
by either public or private troubles.” But whenever my spirit is
roused by reading some brave words, or some noble example spurs me
into action, I want to rush into the law courts, to place my voice
at one man’s disposal, my services at another’s, and to try to help
him even though I may not succeed, or to quell the pride of some
lawyer who is puffed up by ill-deserved success: but I think, by
Hercules, that in philosophical speculation it is better to view
things as they are, and to speak of them on their own account, and
as for words, to trust to things for them, and to let one’s speech
simply follow whither they lead. “Why do you want to construct a
fabric that will endure for ages? Do you not wish to do this in
order that posterity may talk of you: yet you were born to die, and
a silent death is the least wretched.
peace-of-mind_section-01.plainEnglish: I tell myself: "Keep your mind focused on itself and work on improving yourself. Stay out of other people's business. Don't do things just to win approval from others. Enjoy peace that isn't disturbed by public or private problems." But then I read some inspiring words or see a noble example, and my spirit gets fired up. I want to rush into the courtrooms. I want to lend my voice to one person and my services to another. I want to try helping someone, even if I might fail. I want to humble some arrogant lawyer who's gotten cocky from success he doesn't deserve. But honestly, I think it's better in philosophy to see things as they really are and speak about them directly. Trust the facts to supply your words. Let your speech simply follow where the truth leads. "Why do you want to build something that will last forever? Don't you want this so future generations will talk about you? But you were born to die. And a quiet death is the least miserable kind."

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
I have long been silently asking myself, my friend
Serenus, to what I should liken such a condition of mind, and I
find that nothing more closely resembles it than the conduct of
those who, after having recovered from a long and serious illness,
occasionally experience slight touches and twinges, and, although
they have passed through the final stages of the disease, yet have
suspicions that it has not left them, and though in perfect health
yet hold out their pulse to be felt by the physician, and whenever
they feel warm suspect that the fever is returning. Such men,
Serenus, are not unhealthy, but they are not accustomed to being
healthy; just as even a quiet sea or lake nevertheless displays a
certain amount of ripple when its waters are subsiding after a
storm. What you need, therefore, is, not any of those harsher
remedies to which allusion has been made, not that you should in
some cases check yourself, in others be angry with yourself, in
others sternly reproach yourself, but that you should adopt
that which comes last in the list, have confidence in yourself, and
believe that you are proceeding on the right path, without being
led aside by the numerous divergent tracks of wanderers which cross
it in every direction, some of them circling about the right path
itself.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: I've been thinking for a long time, my friend Serenus, about what your state of mind reminds me of. I think it's like people who have recovered from a long, serious illness. They still feel occasional aches and twinges. Even though they got through the worst part of the disease, they suspect it hasn't really left them. They're perfectly healthy now, but they still ask doctors to check their pulse. Whenever they feel warm, they worry the fever is coming back. These people aren't sick, Serenus — they're just not used to being well. It's like how even a calm sea or lake still has some ripples when the water is settling down after a storm. What you need isn't any of those harsh treatments I mentioned before. You don't need to hold yourself back, get angry with yourself, or scold yourself harshly. Instead, you should do what comes last on the list: have confidence in yourself. Believe you're on the right path. Don't let yourself be pulled off course by all the different tracks that confused wanderers have made. These tracks cross everywhere, and some of them even circle around the right path itself.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
What you desire, to be undisturbed, is a great thing, nay,
the greatest thing of all, and one which raises a man almost to the
level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind
_euthymia_, and Democritus’s treatise upon it is excellently written:
I call it peace of mind: for there is no necessity for translating
so exactly as to copy the words of the Greek idiom: the essential
point is to mark the matter under discussion by a name which ought
to have the same meaning as its Greek name, though perhaps not the
same form. What we are seeking, then, is how the mind may always
pursue a steady, unruffled course, may be pleased with itself, and
look with pleasure upon its surroundings, and experience no
interruption of this joy, but abide in a peaceful condition without
being ever either elated or depressed: this will be “peace of mind.”
Let us now consider in a general way how it may be attained: then
you may apply as much as you choose of the universal remedy to your
own case.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: What you want — to be undisturbed — is a great thing. In fact, it's the greatest thing of all. It raises a person almost to the level of a god. The Greeks call this calm steadiness of mind euthymia. Democritus wrote an excellent treatise about it. I call it peace of mind. There's no need to translate so exactly that we copy Greek word forms. The important thing is to give it a name that captures the same meaning, even if the form is different. So what are we looking for? We want the mind to always follow a steady, unruffled path. We want to be pleased with ourselves and look with pleasure at what surrounds us. We want no interruption of this joy. We want to stay in a peaceful state — never getting too high or too low. This is "peace of mind." Now let's think in general terms about how to achieve it. Then you can take whatever you need from this universal remedy and apply it to your own situation.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
Meanwhile we must drag to light the entire disease, and
then each one will recognize his own part of it: at the same time
you will understand how much less you suffer by your self-depreciation
than those who are bound by some showy declaration which they have
made, and are oppressed by some grand title of honour, so that shame
rather than their own free will forces them to keep up the pretence.
The same thing applies both to those who suffer from fickleness and
continual changes of purpose, who always are fondest of what they
have given up, and those who merely yawn and dawdle: add to these
those who, like bad sleepers, turn from side to side, and
settle themselves first in one manner and then in another, until
at last they find rest through sheer weariness: in forming the
habits of their lives they often end by adopting some to which they
are not kept by any dislike of change, but in the practice of which
old age, which is slow to alter, has caught them living: add also
those who are by no means fickle, yet who must thank their dulness,
not their consistency for being so, and who go on living not in the
way they wish, but in the way they have begun to live.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish:
We need to bring this whole disease into the light. Then each person will see their own version of it. You'll realize that your self-doubt causes you much less suffering than those trapped by flashy promises they've made. They're weighed down by grand titles and honors. Shame forces them to keep up the act, not their own choice.

The same goes for people who can't stick to anything. They constantly change their minds and always want what they just gave up. Then there are those who just drift and waste time. Add the ones who toss and turn like restless sleepers. They try one position, then another, until they finally settle down from pure exhaustion. When forming their life habits, they often end up with routines they don't even like. Old age catches them living this way simply because it's slow to change.

Then there are people who aren't fickle at all. But they can thank their dullness for this, not any real consistency. They don't live the way they want — they just live the way they started.

This disease has countless forms, but it has one effect: it makes people unhappy with themselves.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
There are
other special forms of this disease without number, but it has but
one effect, that of making people dissatisfied with themselves.
This arises from a distemperature of mind and from desires which
one is afraid to express or unable to fulfil, when men either dare
not attempt as much as they wish to do, or fail in their efforts
and depend entirely upon hope: such people are always fickle and
changeable, which is a necessary consequence of living in a state
of suspense: they take any way to arrive at their ends, and teach
and force themselves to use both dishonourable and difficult means
to do so, so that when their toil has been in vain they are made
wretched by the disgrace of failure, and do not regret having longed
for what was wrong, but having longed for it in vain.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: This problem comes from an unbalanced mind and desires that people are either afraid to admit or can't fulfill. They either don't dare try for what they want, or they fail and pin everything on hope. These people are always unstable and changeable — which makes sense when you're living in constant suspense. They'll do anything to get what they want. They push themselves to use dishonest and difficult methods. When all that effort fails, they feel miserable about the disgrace of failure. But they don't regret wanting the wrong thing — they regret wanting it uselessly. Then they start feeling sorry for what they've done and become afraid to try again. Their mind gradually falls into endless back-and-forth, because they can neither control nor obey their desires. They hesitate constantly because their life can't develop properly. And they decay as their mind becomes numb from repeated disappointments.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
They then
begin to feel sorry for what they have done, and afraid to begin
again, and their mind falls by degrees into a state of endless
vacillation, because they can neither command nor obey their passions,
of hesitation, because their life cannot properly develope itself,
and of decay, as the mind becomes stupefied by disappointments. All
these symptoms become aggravated when their dislike of a laborious
misery has driven them to idleness and to secret studies, which are
unendurable to a mind eager to take part in public affairs, desirous
of action and naturally restless, because, of course, it finds too
few resources within itself: when therefore it loses the amusement
which business itself affords to busy men, it cannot endure
home, loneliness, or the walls of a room, and regards itself with
dislike when left to itself. Hence arises that weariness and
dissatisfaction with oneself, that tossing to and fro of a mind
which can nowhere find rest, that unhappy and unwilling endurance
of enforced leisure. In all cases where one feels ashamed to confess
the real cause of one’s suffering, and where modesty leads one to
drive one’s sufferings inward, the desires pent up in a little space
without any vent choke one another. Hence comes melancholy and
drooping of spirit, and a thousand waverings of the unsteadfast
mind, which is held in suspense by unfulfilled hopes, and saddened
by disappointed ones: hence comes the state of mind of those who
loathe their idleness, complain that they have nothing to do, and
view the progress of others with the bitterest jealousy: for an
unhappy sloth favours the growth of envy, and men who cannot succeed
themselves wish every one else to be ruined.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish:
All these problems get worse when people hate hard work so much that they retreat into idleness and private studies. But minds that crave public life and action can't stand this isolation. They need external stimulation because they have too few inner resources. When they lose the entertainment that comes from staying busy, they can't bear being at home, alone, or stuck in a room. They start to dislike themselves when left with only their own company.

This creates that restless dissatisfaction with yourself. Your mind tosses back and forth, unable to find peace anywhere. You hate being forced into leisure but feel stuck with it. When you're too embarrassed to admit what's really bothering you, and pride makes you bottle up your pain, all those trapped desires choke each other in the confined space of your mind. This leads to depression and despair, and endless wavering of an unstable mind suspended between unfulfilled hopes and crushed disappointments.

This is why people who hate their own idleness complain they have nothing to do, then watch other people's success with bitter jealousy. Miserable laziness breeds envy. When you can't succeed yourself, you want everyone else to fail too.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
This dislike of other
men’s progress and despair of one’s own produces a mind angered
against fortune, addicted to complaining of the age in which it
lives, to retiring into corners and brooding over its misery, until
it becomes sick and weary of itself: for the human mind is naturally
nimble and apt at movement: it delights in every opportunity of
excitement and forgetfulness of itself, and the worse a man’s
disposition the more he delights in this, because he likes to wear
himself out with busy action, just as some sores long for the hands
that injure them and delight in being touched, and the foul itch
enjoys anything that scratches it. Similarly I assure you that these
minds, over which desires have spread like evil ulcers, take pleasure
in toils and troubles, for there are some things which please our
body while at the same time they give it a certain amount of pain,
such as turning oneself over and changing one’s side before it is
wearied, or cooling oneself in one position after another.
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish:
When we resent other people's success and feel hopeless about our own, our minds turn bitter against fortune. We complain about the times we live in. We retreat into corners and brood over our misery until we become sick of ourselves.

The human mind naturally wants to move and be active. It loves any chance to get excited and forget itself. The worse someone's character, the more they crave this distraction. They want to wear themselves out with constant activity — like a wound that craves the very hands that hurt it, or an itch that enjoys being scratched.

I'm telling you, minds infected by desire act like festering ulcers. They actually enjoy stress and trouble. Some things feel good to our bodies even while causing pain — like tossing and turning in bed, or shifting positions to get cool. It's like Homer's Achilles, lying face down, then on his back, constantly changing positions. Like sick people do, he can't stand any position for long. He keeps moving, thinking change itself will cure him.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
It is
like Homer’s Achilles, lying first upon its face, then upon
its back, placing itself in various attitudes, and, as sick people
are wont, enduring none of them for long, and using changes as
though they were remedies. Hence men undertake aimless wanderings,
travel along distant shores, and at one time at sea, at another by
land, try to soothe that fickleness of disposition which always is
dissatisfied with the present. “Now let us make for Campania: now
I am sick of rich cultivation: let us see wild regions, let us
thread the passes of Bruttii and Lucania: yet amid this wilderness
one wants something of beauty to relieve our pampered eyes after
so long dwelling on savage wastes: let us seek Tarentum with its
famous harbour, its mild winter climate, and its district, rich
enough to support even the great hordes of ancient times. Let us
now return to town: our ears have too long missed its shouts and
noise: it would be pleasant also to enjoy the sight of human
bloodshed.” Thus one journey succeeds another, and one sight is
changed for another. As Lucretius says:—
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: So people wander around without purpose. They travel to distant places. Sometimes by sea, sometimes by land. They're trying to calm their restless minds, which are never satisfied with where they are now. "Let's go to Campania! No wait, I'm tired of all this fancy farmland. Let's see wild places instead. Let's hike through the mountains of Bruttii and Lucania. But even in this wilderness, I need something beautiful to look at — my spoiled eyes are tired of all this rough country. Let's go to Tarentum with its famous harbor, mild winters, and rich land that could feed huge armies back in ancient times. Actually, let's go back to the city. I miss the shouting and noise. It would be fun to watch some gladiator fights too." So one trip leads to another. One sight gets swapped for another. As Lucretius said: "Everyone runs away from himself." But what's the point? You can't escape from yourself. You follow yourself everywhere and drag yourself down with your own terrible company.

peace-of-mind_section-02.originalText:
“Thus every mortal from himself doth flee;”

but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself?
he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome
companionship. We must understand, therefore, that what we suffer
from is not the fault of the places but of ourselves: we are weak
when there is anything to be endured, and cannot support either
labour or pleasure, either one’s own business or any one else’s for
long. This has driven some men to death, because by frequently
altering their purpose they were always brought back to the same
point, and had left themselves no room for anything new. They had
become sick of life and of the world itself, and as all indulgences
palled upon them they began to ask themselves the question, “How
long are we to go on doing the same thing?”
peace-of-mind_section-02.plainEnglish: We need to understand that our suffering isn't the fault of our surroundings — it's our own fault. We're weak when we have to endure anything. We can't handle hard work or pleasure for long. We can't stick with our own projects or other people's projects either. This restlessness has driven some people to suicide. They kept changing their minds and goals, but always ended up back where they started. They left themselves no room for anything new. They got sick of life and the world itself. When all their pleasures became boring, they started asking themselves: 'How long do we have to keep doing the same thing over and over?'

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText:
You ask me what I think we had better make use of to help us
to support this ennui. “The best thing,” as Athenodorus says, “is
to occupy oneself with business with the management of affairs of
state and the duties of a citizen: for as some pass the day in
exercising themselves in the sun and in taking care of their bodily
health, and athletes find it most useful to spend the greater part
of their time in feeding up the muscles and strength to whose
cultivation they have devoted their lives; so too for you who are
training your mind to take part in the struggles of political life,
it is far more honourable to be thus at work than to be idle. He
whose object is to be of service to his countrymen and to all
mortals, exercises himself and does good at the same time when he
is engrossed in business and is working to the best of his ability
both in the interests of the public and of private men. But,”
continues he, “because innocence is hardly safe among such furious
ambitions and so many men who turn one aside from the right path,
and it is always sure to meet with more hindrance than help, we
ought to withdraw ourselves from the forum and from public life,
and a great mind even in a private station can find room wherein
to expand freely.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: You ask me what I think we should use to fight off this boredom and restlessness. "The best remedy," as Athenodorus says, "is to keep yourself busy with real work — managing public affairs and doing your duties as a citizen. Some people spend their days exercising in the sun and taking care of their bodies. Athletes find it most helpful to spend most of their time building up the muscles and strength they've devoted their lives to developing. In the same way, if you're training your mind for the struggles of political life, it's far more honorable to be working than sitting around idle. A person who wants to serve his fellow citizens and all humanity exercises himself and does good at the same time. When he's absorbed in important work and doing his best for both the public and private individuals, he's helping himself and others."

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText:
Confinement in dens restrains the springs of lions
and wild creatures, but this does not apply to human beings, who
often effect the most important works in retirement. Let a man,
however, withdraw himself only in such a fashion that wherever he
spends his leisure his wish may still be to benefit individual men
and mankind alike, both with his intellect, his voice, and his
advice. The man that does good service to the state is not only he
who brings forward candidates for public office, defends accused
persons, and gives his vote on questions of peace and war, but he
who encourages young men in well-doing, who supplies the present
dearth of good teachers by instilling into their minds the principles
of virtue, who seizes and holds back those who are rushing
wildly in pursuit of riches and luxury, and, if he does nothing
else, at least checks their course—such a man does service to the
public though in a private station.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: But he continues, "Staying innocent is nearly impossible when people are so hungry for power and so many try to lead you astray. You'll face more obstacles than help. So we should pull back from politics and public life. Even a great mind can find room to grow in private life. Caging lions and wild animals breaks their spirit, but this doesn't apply to humans. We often do our most important work when we step away from the crowd. But when you do withdraw, make sure you still want to help both individuals and humanity as a whole — with your mind, your words, and your counsel."

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText:
Which does the most good, he
who decides between foreigners and citizens (as praetor peregrinus),
or, as praetor urbanus, pronounces sentence to the suitors in his
court at his assistant’s dictation, or he who shows them what is
meant by justice, filial feeling, endurance, courage, contempt of
death and knowledge of the gods, and how much a man is helped by a
good conscience? If then you transfer to philosophy the time which
you take away from the public service, you will not be a deserter
or have refused to perform your proper task. A soldier is not merely
one who stands in the ranks and defends the right or the left wing
of the army, but he also who guards the gates—a service which,
though less dangerous, is no sinecure—who keeps watch, and takes
charge of the arsenal: though all these are bloodless duties, yet
they count as military service.
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: The man who serves the state isn't just someone who nominates people for office, defends the accused in court, or votes on war and peace. He also serves when he encourages young people to do right. He serves when he makes up for the shortage of good teachers by teaching virtue. He serves when he stops people who are frantically chasing money and luxury — or at least slows them down. This man serves the public even though he holds no office. Who does more good? The judge who settles disputes between foreigners and citizens, or the one who reads verdicts dictated by his clerk? Or the man who teaches what justice really means — along with devotion to family, endurance, courage, acceptance of death, and understanding of the gods? Who shows how much a clear conscience can help you?

peace-of-mind_section-03.originalText:
As soon as you have devoted yourself
to philosophy, you will have overcome all disgust at life: you will
not wish for darkness because you are weary of the light, nor will
you be a trouble to yourself and useless to others: you will acquire
many friends, and all the best men will be attracted towards you:
for virtue, in however obscure a position, cannot be hidden, but
gives signs of its presence: any one who is worthy will trace it
out by its footsteps: but if we give up all society, turn our backs
upon the whole human race, and live communing with ourselves alone,
this solitude without any interesting occupation will lead to a
want of something to do: we shall begin to build up and to pull
down, to dam out the sea, to cause waters to flow through natural
obstacles, and generally to make a bad disposal of the time which
Nature has given us to spend: some of us use it grudgingly, others
wastefully; some of us spend it so that we can show a profit and
loss account, others so that they have no assets remaining:
than which nothing can be more shameful. Often a man who is very
old in years has nothing beyond his age by which he can prove that
he has lived a long time.”
peace-of-mind_section-03.plainEnglish: If you take the time you would have spent on public service and give it to philosophy instead, you won't be a deserter or someone who refused to do his duty. A soldier isn't just someone who stands in formation and defends the army's flanks. He's also the one who guards the gates — a job that's less dangerous but still real work. He keeps watch and manages the weapons. These duties don't involve bloodshed, but they still count as military service. Once you commit yourself to philosophy, you'll overcome any disgust with life. You won't wish for darkness because you're tired of the light. You won't be a burden to yourself or useless to others. You'll gain many friends, and all the best people will be drawn to you. Virtue can't be hidden, no matter how humble your position. It always shows signs of itself. Anyone worthy of it will track it down by following its trail.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText:
To me, my dearest Serenus, Athenodorus seems to have yielded
too completely to the times, to have fled too soon: I will not deny
that sometimes one must retire, but one ought to retire slowly, at
a foot’s pace, without losing one’s ensigns or one’s honour as a
soldier: those who make terms with arms in their hands are more
respected by their enemies and more safe in their hands. This is
what I think ought to be done by virtue and by one who practises
virtue: if Fortune get the upper hand and deprive him of the power
of action, let him not straightway turn his back to the enemy, throw
away his arms, and run away seeking for a hiding-place, as if there
were any place whither Fortune could not pursue him, but let him
be more sparing in his acceptance of public office, and after due
deliberation discover some means by which he can be of use to the
state. He is not able to serve in the army: then let him become a
candidate for civic honours: must he live in a private station?
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish:
My dear Serenus, I think Athenodorus gave up too easily. He retreated too quickly from public life. I won't deny that sometimes you need to step back. But you should retreat slowly, with dignity. Keep your standards high and your honor intact. Soldiers who negotiate while still holding their weapons get more respect from their enemies. They're also safer.

This is what virtue should do. This is what anyone trying to live well should do. If Fortune gets the upper hand and blocks your ability to act, don't immediately turn and run. Don't throw down your weapons and hide. There's no place Fortune can't find you anyway. Instead, be more careful about taking on public roles. Think it through. Find some way you can still serve your country.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText:
then let him be an advocate: is he condemned to keep silence? then
let him help his countrymen with silent counsel. Is it dangerous
for him even to enter the forum? then let him prove himself a good
comrade, a faithful friend, a sober guest in people’s houses, at
public shows, and at wine-parties. Suppose that he has lost the
status of a citizen; then let him exercise that of a man: our reason
for magnanimously refusing to confine ourselves within the walls
of one city, for having gone forth to enjoy intercourse with all
lands and for professing ourselves to be citizens of the world is
that we may thus obtain a wider theatre on which to display our
virtue. Is the bench of judges closed to you, are you forbidden to
address the people from the hustings, or to be a candidate at
elections? then turn your eyes away from Rome, and see what
a wide extent of territory, what a number of nations present
themselves before you.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish: Can't serve in the army? Then run for public office. Must live as a private citizen? Then become a lawyer. Are you forced to stay silent? Then help your fellow citizens with quiet advice. Is it dangerous to even enter the public square? Then be a good companion, a loyal friend, a well-behaved guest in homes, at public events, and at parties. Have you lost your citizenship? Then act like a human being. We proudly refuse to limit ourselves to one city. We go out to connect with all lands and call ourselves citizens of the world. Why? So we have a bigger stage to show our virtue.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText:
Thus, it is never possible for so many outlets
to be closed against your ambition that more will not remain open
to it: but see whether the whole prohibition does not arise from
your own fault. You do not choose to direct the affairs of the state
except as consul or prytanis[2] or meddix[3] or sufes:[4] what
should we say if you refused to serve in the army save as general
or military tribune? Even though others may form the first line,
and your lot may have placed you among the veterans of the third,
do your duty there with your voice, encouragement, example, and
spirit: even though a man’s hands be cut off, he may find means to
help his side in a battle, if he stands his ground and cheers on
his comrades. Do something of that sort yourself: if Fortune removes
you from the front rank, stand your ground nevertheless and cheer
on your comrades, and if somebody stops your mouth, stand nevertheless
and help your side in silence.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish:
Are you banned from being a judge? Can't you speak to the people or run for office? Then look beyond Rome. See how much territory there is, how many nations stretch before you. It's impossible for every door to your ambitions to be shut — there are always more paths open. But ask yourself: is this ban really your own fault?

You refuse to serve the state unless you can be consul or some other high official. What if someone refused to serve in the army unless they could be a general or officer? Even if others form the front line and fate puts you with the veterans in back, do your duty there. Use your voice, give encouragement, set an example, show your spirit. Even a man with his hands cut off can help his side in battle if he stands firm and cheers on his comrades.

peace-of-mind_section-04.originalText:
The services of a good citizen are
never thrown away: he does good by being heard and seen, by his
expression, his gestures, his silent determination, and his very
walk. As some remedies benefit us by their smell as well as by their
their taste and touch, so virtue even when concealed and at a
distance sheds usefulness around. Whether she moves at her ease and
enjoys her just rights, or can only appear abroad on sufferance and
is forced to shorten sail to the tempest, whether it be unemployed,
silent, and pent up in a narrow lodging, or openly displayed, in
whatever guise she may appear, she always does good. What? do you
think that the example of one who can rest nobly has no value? It
is by far the best plan, therefore, to mingle leisure with
business, whenever chance impediments or the state of public affairs
forbid one’s leading an active life: for one is never so cut off
from all pursuits as to find no room left for honourable action.
peace-of-mind_section-04.plainEnglish: Do something like that yourself. If fortune pushes you out of the spotlight, hold your ground anyway and cheer on your teammates. If someone silences you, still stand there and help your side quietly. The work of a good citizen is never wasted. He helps just by being heard and seen — through his face, his gestures, his quiet strength, even the way he walks. Some medicines help us through their smell as well as their taste and touch. Virtue works the same way. Even when it's hidden or far away, it spreads usefulness around. Whether virtue moves freely and enjoys its proper place, or has to appear carefully and pull back during storms, whether it sits unused and silent in tight quarters, or shows itself openly — whatever form it takes, it always does good. Do you really think there's no value in someone who knows how to rest with dignity? The best plan is to mix rest with work. When obstacles or public troubles prevent you from living an active life, you're never so cut off that there's no room left for honorable action.

peace-of-mind_section-05.originalText:
Could you anywhere find a [more] miserable city than that of
Athens when it was being torn to pieces by the thirty tyrants? they
slew thirteen hundred citizens, all the best men, and did not leave
off because they had done so, but their cruelty became stimulated
by exercise. In the city which possessed that most reverend tribunal,
the Court of the Areopagus, which possessed a Senate, and a popular
assembly which was like a Senate, there met daily a wretched crew
of butchers, and the unhappy Senate House was crowded with tyrants.
A state, in which there were so many tyrants that they would have
been enough to form a bodyguard for one, might surely have rested
from the struggle; it seemed impossible for men’s minds even to
conceive hopes of recovering their liberty, nor could they see any
room for a remedy for such a mass of evil: for whence could the
unhappy state obtain all the Harmodiuses it would need to slay so
many tyrants? Yet Socrates was in the midst of the city, and consoled
its mourning Fathers, encouraged those who despaired of the republic,
by his reproaches brought rich men, who feared that their wealth
would be their ruin, to a tardy repentance of their avarice, and
moved about as a great example to those who wished to imitate him,
because he walked a free man in the midst of thirty masters.
peace-of-mind_section-05.plainEnglish: Could you find anywhere a more miserable city than Athens when it was being torn apart by the thirty tyrants? They killed thirteen hundred citizens — all the best men — and didn't stop there. Their cruelty only grew stronger with practice. In the city that had the respected Areopagus court, that had a Senate and a popular assembly like a Senate, a wretched crew of butchers met daily. The unhappy Senate House was packed with tyrants. When a state had so many tyrants that they could have formed a bodyguard for one ruler, it seemed the struggle should have ended. It seemed impossible for people's minds even to imagine getting their freedom back. They couldn't see any way to fix such a mountain of evil. Where could the unhappy state find enough heroes like Harmodius to kill so many tyrants?

peace-of-mind_section-05.originalText:
However,
Athens herself put him to death in prison, and Freedom herself could
not endure the freedom of one who had treated a whole band of tyrants
with scorn: you may know, therefore, that even in an oppressed state
a wise man can find an opportunity for bringing himself to the
front, and that in a prosperous and flourishing one wanton insolence,
jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly vices bear sway. We ought,
therefore, to expand or contract ourselves according as the
state presents itself to us, or as Fortune offers us opportunities:
but in any case we ought to move and not to become frozen still by
fear: nay, he is the best man who, though peril menaces him on every
side and arms and chains beset his path, nevertheless neither impairs
nor conceals his virtue: for to keep oneself safe does not mean to
bury oneself. I think that Curius Dentatus spoke truly when he said
that he would rather be dead than alive: the worst evil of all is
to leave the ranks of the living before one dies: yet it is your
duty, if you happen to live in an age when it is not easy to serve
the state, to devote more time to leisure and to literature. Thus,
just as though you were making a perilous voyage, you may from time
to time put into harbour, and set yourself free from public business
without waiting for it to do so.
peace-of-mind_section-05.plainEnglish: Yet Socrates lived right in the heart of the city. He comforted grieving leaders and encouraged those who had given up hope for their country. He shamed wealthy men who feared their riches would destroy them, pushing them to finally regret their greed. He walked around as a living example for anyone who wanted to follow his path. Here was a free man walking among thirty tyrants. But Athens itself killed him in prison. Even Freedom couldn't stand the freedom of a man who had mocked an entire gang of dictators. So you can see that even in a crushed state, a wise person can find ways to make a difference. But in a successful and thriving state, reckless arrogance, jealousy, and a thousand other cowardly flaws rule the day.

peace-of-mind_section-06.originalText:
We ought, however, first to examine our own selves, next the
business which we propose to transact, next those for whose sake
or in whose company we transact it.
peace-of-mind_section-06.plainEnglish:
We should examine three things before we act. First, ourselves. Second, the task we want to do. Third, the people we'll be working with or for.

Most importantly, we need to know ourselves honestly. We usually think we can do more than we actually can. One person gets carried away by his speaking ability. Another expects his money to earn more than it possibly can. Someone else pushes his weak body to do hard physical work. Some people are too shy for politics, which requires thick skin. Others are too stubborn and proud for court life. Some can't control their temper and say reckless things when they get upset. Others can't resist making dangerous jokes, even when it's risky. For all these people, staying out of public life is better than jumping in. If you're bold, arrogant, and impatient, avoid anything that might tempt you to speak too freely. That kind of talk will destroy you.

peace-of-mind_section-06.originalText:
It is above all things necessary to form a true estimate of oneself,
because as a rule we think that we can do more than we are able:
one man is led too far through confidence in his eloquence, another
demands more from his estate than it can produce, another burdens
a weakly body with some toilsome duty. Some men are too shamefaced
for the conduct of public affairs, which require an unblushing
front: some men’s obstinate pride renders them unfit for courts:
some cannot control their anger, and break into unguarded language
on the slightest provocation: some cannot rein in their wit or
resist making risky jokes: for all these men leisure is better than
employment: a bold, haughty and impatient nature ought to avoid
anything that may lead it to use a freedom of speech which will
bring it to ruin. Next we must form an estimate of the matter which
we mean to deal with, and compare our strength with the deed
we are about to attempt: for the bearer ought always to be more
powerful than his load: indeed, loads which are too heavy for their
bearer must of necessity crush him: some affairs also are not so
important in themselves as they are prolific and lead to much more
business, which employments, as they involve us in new and various
forms of work, ought to be refused. Neither should you engage in
anything from which you are not free to retreat: apply yourself to
something which you can finish, or at any rate can hope to finish:
you had better not meddle with those operations which grow in
importance, while they are being transacted, and which will not
stop where you intended them to stop.
peace-of-mind_section-06.plainEnglish: Next, we need to think carefully about what we're taking on. We need to compare our strength with the task we're about to attempt. The person carrying a load should always be stronger than what they're carrying. If a load is too heavy, it will definitely crush the person carrying it. Some projects aren't just big in themselves — they multiply and lead to much more work. You should refuse these jobs because they drag you into new and different kinds of work. Don't start anything you can't walk away from. Focus on something you can finish, or at least something you can hope to finish. It's better to avoid projects that grow bigger while you're working on them — projects that won't stop where you planned them to stop.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText:
In all cases one should be careful in one’s choice of men, and
see whether they be worthy of our bestowing a part of our life upon
them, or whether we shall waste our own time and theirs also: for
some even consider us to be in their debt because of our services
to them. Athenodorus said that “he would not so much as dine with
a man who would not be grateful to him for doing so”: meaning, I
imagine, that much less would he go to dinner with those who
recompense the services of their friends by their table, and regard
courses of dishes as donatives, as if they overate themselves to
do honour to others. Take away from these men their witnesses and
spectators: they will take no pleasure in solitary gluttony. You
must decide whether your disposition is better suited for vigorous
action or for tranquil speculation and contemplation, and you must
adopt whichever the bent of your genius inclines you for.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: You need to choose your friends carefully. Ask yourself: are they worth giving part of your life to? Or will you just waste your time and theirs? Some people actually think you owe them something when you do them favors. Athenodorus said he wouldn't even have dinner with someone who wasn't grateful for the invitation. He meant that he definitely wouldn't dine with people who think a fancy meal repays their friends' kindness — people who treat expensive dishes like generous gifts, as if stuffing themselves somehow honors their guests. Take away their audience and witnesses, and these people won't enjoy eating alone at all.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText:
Isocrates
laid hands upon Ephorus and led him away from the forum, thinking
that he would be more usefully employed in compiling chronicles;
for no good is done by forcing one’s mind to engage in uncongenial
work: it is vain to struggle against Nature. Yet nothing delights
the mind so much as faithful and pleasant friendship: what a
blessing it is when there is one whose breast is ready to receive
all your secrets with safety, whose knowledge of your actions you
fear less than your own conscience, whose conversation removes your
anxieties, whose advice assists your plans, whose cheerfulness
dispels your gloom, whose very sight delights you! We should choose
for our friends men who are, as far as possible, free from strong
desires: for vices are contagious, and pass from a man to his
neighbour, and injure those who touch them.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: You need to figure out what suits you better: taking action in the world or quiet thinking and study. Then follow whichever path your natural talents point you toward. Isocrates pulled his student Ephorus away from public speaking and got him to write history instead. He knew Ephorus would do better work that way. There's no point in forcing your mind to do work it's not built for. You can't win a fight against your own nature.

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText:
As, therefore, in times
of pestilence we have to be careful not to sit near people who are
infected and in whom the disease is raging, because by so doing,
we shall run into danger and catch the plague from their very breath;
so, too, in choosing our friends’ dispositions, we must take care
to select those who are as far as may be unspotted by the world;
for the way to breed disease is to mix what is sound with what is
rotten. Yet I do not advise you to follow after or draw to yourself
no one except a wise man: for where will you find him whom for so
many centuries we have sought in vain? in the place of the best
possible man take him who is least bad.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: Nothing brings more joy to the mind than true and delightful friendship. What a gift it is to have someone you can trust with all your secrets — someone whose judgment you fear less than your own conscience. Their conversation eases your worries. Their advice helps your plans. Their cheerfulness lifts your spirits. Just seeing them makes you happy!

peace-of-mind_section-07.originalText:
You would hardly find any
time that would have enabled you to make a happier choice than if
you could have sought for a good man from among the Platos and
Xenophons and the rest of the produce of the brood of Socrates, or
if you had been permitted to choose one from the age of Cato: an
age which bore many men worthy to be born in Cato’s time (just as
it also bore many men worse than were ever known before, planners
of the blackest crimes: for it needed both classes in order to make
Cato understood: it wanted both good men, that he might win their
approbation, and bad men, against whom he could prove his strength):
but at the present day, when there is such a dearth of good men,
you must be less squeamish in your choice. Above all, however, avoid
dismal men who grumble at whatever happens, and find something to
complain of in everything. Though he may continue loyal and
friendly towards you, still one’s peace of mind is destroyed by a
comrade whose mind is soured and who meets every incident with a
groan.
peace-of-mind_section-07.plainEnglish: We should choose friends who are free from strong desires as much as possible. Vices spread like diseases. They pass from person to person and harm anyone who gets close. During a plague, we're careful not to sit near infected people whose disease is raging. We know we'll catch it from their breath if we do. We need the same care when choosing friends. We must pick people who are as untainted as possible. The surest way to create disease is to mix what is healthy with what is rotten.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText:
Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that
most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the
other ills from which we suffer—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets,
endurance of pains and labours— with those miseries which our money
inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others.
Reflect, then, how much less a grief it is never to have had any
money than to have lost it: we shall thus understand that the less
poverty has to lose, the less torment it has with which to afflict
us: for you are mistaken if you suppose that the rich bear their
losses with greater spirit than the poor: a wound causes the same
amount of pain to the greatest and the smallest body.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Now let's talk about money and possessions — the biggest source of human misery. If you compare all our other troubles — death, illness, fear, regret, pain, hard work — with the problems that money causes us, money wins by a landslide. Think about this: it hurts much less to never have money than to lose money you once had. This shows us that the less poor people have to lose, the less they can be tortured by loss. You're wrong if you think rich people handle financial losses better than poor people do. A wound hurts the same whether you're big or small. Bion had a clever way of putting it: "Pulling out hair hurts just as much whether you're bald or have a full head of hair." The same is true for rich and poor people — they suffer equally when they lose money. Money sticks to both types of people, and you can't rip it away without them feeling it. But as I said, it's easier to bear never getting something than losing something you had. That's why you'll notice that people who were never lucky are often happier than people who used to be lucky but aren't anymore.

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText:
It was a neat
saying of Bion’s, “that it hurts bald men as much as hairy men to
have their hairs pulled out”: you may be assured that the same thing
is true of rich and poor people, that their suffering is equal: for
their money clings to both classes, and cannot be torn away without
their feeling it: yet it is more endurable, as I have said, and
easier not to gain property than to lose it, and therefore you will
find that those upon whom Fortune has never smiled are more cheerful
than those whom she has deserted. Diogenes, a man of infinite spirit,
perceived this, and made it impossible that anything should be taken
from him. Call this security from loss poverty, want, necessity,
or any contemptuous name you please: I shall consider such a man
to be happy, unless you find me another who can lose nothing. If I
am not mistaken, it is a royal attribute among so many misers,
sharpers, and robbers, to be the one man who cannot be injured. If
any one doubts the happiness of Diogenes, he would doubt whether
the position of the immortal gods was one of sufficient happiness.
because they have no farms or gardens, no valuable estates
let to strange tenants, and no large loans in the money market.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: Diogenes was a man of great spirit who figured this out. He made it impossible for anyone to take anything from him. Call this freedom from loss whatever you want — poverty, want, necessity, or any insulting name you can think of. I still say this man was happy, unless you can show me another person who has nothing to lose. If I'm right, then among all the greedy people, cheaters, and thieves in the world, being the one person who can't be harmed is almost godlike. Anyone who doubts Diogenes was happy might as well doubt whether the gods themselves are happy enough — after all, they don't own farms or gardens, they don't have valuable estates rented out to tenants, and they don't have big investments in the money market. Aren't you ashamed of yourself for staring at wealth with such amazement? Look at the universe: you'll see the gods own absolutely nothing, yet they give us everything. Do you really think this man who stripped away all the random things fortune gives us is poor? Or is he more like the immortal gods?

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText:
Are
you not ashamed of yourself, you who gaze upon riches with astonished
admiration? Look upon the universe: you will see the gods quite
bare of property, and possessing nothing though they give everything.
Do you think that this man who has stripped himself of all fortuitous
accessories is a pauper, or one like to the immortal gods? Do you
call Demetrius, Pompeius’s freedman, a happier man, he who was not
ashamed to be richer than Pompeius, who was daily furnished with a
list of the number of his slaves, as a general is with that of his
army, though he had long deserved that all his riches should consist
of a pair of underlings, and a roomier cell than the other slaves?
But Diogenes’s only slave ran away from him, and when he was pointed
out to Diogenes, he did not think him worth fetching back. “It is
a shame,” he said, “that Manes should be able to live without
Diogenes, and that Diogenes should not be able to live without
Manes.” He seems to me to have said, “Fortune, mind your own business:
Diogenes has nothing left that belongs to you.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish:
Do you think Demetrius was happier? He was Pompey's former slave who became incredibly wealthy. He wasn't even embarrassed that he had more money than Pompey himself. Every day someone brought him a count of how many slaves he owned, like a general getting a report on his army. But really, he deserved nothing more than two assistants and a slightly bigger prison cell than the other slaves.

Compare that to Diogenes. His one slave ran away. When someone pointed the runaway out to him, Diogenes didn't think the man was worth chasing down. "It would be shameful," he said, "if Manes can live without Diogenes, but Diogenes can't live without Manes." It's like he was telling Fortune: "Mind your own business! You have no power over Diogenes anymore. Did my slave run away? No — he left me as a free man."

peace-of-mind_section-08.originalText:
Did my slave run
away? nay, he went away from me as a free man.” A household of
slaves requires food and clothing: the bellies of so many hungry
creatures have to be filled: we must buy raiment for them, we must
watch their most thievish hands, and we must make use of the services
of people who weep and execrate us. How far happier is he who is
indebted to no man for anything except for what he can deprive
himself of with the greatest ease! Since we, however, have not such
strength of mind as this, we ought at any rate to diminish the
extent of our property, in order to be less exposed to the assaults
of fortune: those men whose bodies can be within the shelter of
their armour, are more fitted for war than those whose huge size
everywhere extends beyond it, and exposes them to wounds: the
best amount of property to have is that which is enough to keep us
from poverty, and which yet is not far removed from it.
peace-of-mind_section-08.plainEnglish: A household full of slaves needs food and clothes. You have to feed all those hungry mouths. You have to buy them clothing and watch their thieving hands. And you have to rely on people who hate you and curse your name. How much happier is the person who owes nothing to anyone — except for things he could easily give up! Since most of us don't have that kind of mental strength, we should at least cut down on our possessions. This way we're less exposed to fortune's attacks. Soldiers who can fit inside their armor are better prepared for war than those whose huge bodies stick out everywhere, making them easy targets. The best amount of wealth is just enough to keep you out of poverty — but not much more than that.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText:
We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have
previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are
sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the
remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid
of thrift can convert itself into riches. Let us accustom ourselves
to set aside mere outward show, and to measure things by their uses,
not by their ornamental trappings: let our hunger be tamed by food,
our thirst quenched by drinking, our lust confined within needful
bounds; let us learn to use our limbs, and to arrange our dress and
way of life according to what was approved of by our ancestors, not
in imitation of new-fangled models: let us learn to increase our
continence, to repress luxury, to set bounds to our pride, to assuage
our anger, to look upon poverty without prejudice, to practise
thrift, albeit many are ashamed to do so, to apply cheap remedies
to the wants of nature, to keep all undisciplined hopes and aspirations
as it were under lock and key, and to make it our business to get
our riches from ourselves and not from Fortune.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish:
We'll be happy with whatever money we have if we first learn to enjoy living simply. Without that, no amount of wealth is ever enough. With it, no amount is too little. The cure is always within reach — even poverty can become wealth if you add thrift to it.

Let's get used to ignoring flashy appearances. Judge things by how useful they are, not by how fancy they look. Let food satisfy our hunger, drinks quench our thirst, and our desires stay within reasonable limits. Let's learn to use our bodies properly and dress the way our ancestors did — not copying every new trend.

Let's practice more self-control. Cut back on luxury. Put limits on our pride. Calm our anger. Look at poverty without bias. Practice thrift, even though many people are embarrassed by it. Use simple, cheap solutions for our basic needs. Keep all our wild hopes and ambitions locked up tight. Make it our job to get our wealth from ourselves, not from luck.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText:
We never can so
thoroughly defeat the vast diversity and malignity of misfortune
with which we are threatened as not to feel the weight of many gusts
if we offer a large spread of canvas to the wind: we must draw our
affairs into a small compass, to make the darts of Fortune of no
avail. For this reason, sometimes slight mishaps have turned into
remedies, and more serious disorders have been healed by slighter
ones. When the mind pays no attention to good advice, and cannot
be brought to its senses by milder measures, why should we not think
that its interests are being served by poverty, disgrace, or financial
ruin being applied to it? one evil is balanced by another. Let us
then teach ourselves to be able to dine without all Rome to
look on, to be the slaves of fewer slaves, to get clothes which
fulfil their original purpose, and to live in a smaller house.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: We can never completely defeat all the bad luck that threatens us. If we spread our sails too wide, we'll feel the force of every gust. We need to keep our lives simple and small so fortune's arrows can't hit us. Sometimes small setbacks actually help us. Sometimes bigger problems get cured by smaller ones. When your mind won't listen to good advice and gentle methods don't work, maybe poverty, shame, or financial ruin is exactly what it needs. One bad thing cancels out another. So let's learn to eat dinner without all of Rome watching. Let's have fewer servants to serve us. Let's wear clothes that just keep us warm and dry. Let's live in smaller houses. In horse racing and in life, you win by taking the inside track — the shortest path.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText:
The
inner curve is the one to take, not only in running races and in
the contests of the circus, but also in the race of life; even
literary pursuits, the most becoming thing for a gentleman to spend
money upon, are only justifiable as long as they are kept within
bounds. What is the use of possessing numberless books and libraries,
whose titles their owner can hardly read through in a lifetime? A
student is overwhelmed by such a mass, not instructed, and it is
much better to devote yourself to a few writers than to skim through
many. Forty thousand books were burned at Alexandria: some would
have praised this library as a most noble memorial of royal wealth,
like Titus Livius, who says that it was “a splendid result of the
taste and attentive care of the kings.”[5] It had nothing to do
with taste or care, but was a piece of learned luxury, nay, not
even learned, since they amassed it, not for the sake of learning,
but to make a show, like many men who know less about letters than
a slave is expected to know, and who uses his books not to help him
in his studies but to ornament his dining-room.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: Even book collecting — the most respectable way for a gentleman to spend money — only makes sense if you keep it reasonable. What's the point of owning countless books and libraries when you can barely read all the titles in a lifetime? A huge collection overwhelms you instead of teaching you anything. It's much better to focus on a few good writers than to skim through hundreds. Forty thousand books burned at Alexandria. Some people, like the historian Livy, praised that library as "a splendid monument to royal taste and care." But it had nothing to do with taste or care. It was just scholarly showing off — and not even scholarly, since they collected books to impress people, not to learn from them. Like many people today who know less about literature than their servants do, and use their books to decorate their dining rooms instead of actually studying them.

peace-of-mind_section-09.originalText:
Let a man, then,
obtain as many books as he wants, but none for show. “It is more
respectable,” say you, “to spend one’s money on such books than on
vases of Corinthian brass and paintings.” Not so: everything that
is carried to excess is wrong. What excuses can you find for a man
who is eager to buy bookcases of ivory and citrus wood, to collect
the works of unknown or discredited authors, and who sits yawning
amid so many thousands of books, whose backs and titles please
him more than any other part of them? Thus in the houses of the
laziest of men you will see the works of all the orators and
historians stacked upon book-shelves reaching right up to the
ceiling. At the present day a library has become as necessary an
appendage to a house as a hot and cold bath. I would excuse them
straightway if they really were carried away by an excessive zeal
for literature; but as it is, these costly works of sacred genius,
with all the illustrations that adorn them, are merely bought for
display and to serve as wall-furniture.
peace-of-mind_section-09.plainEnglish: Get as many books as you want, but don't buy them just to show off. "It's more respectable," you say, "to spend money on books than on fancy bronze vases and paintings." Wrong. Anything taken to extremes is a mistake. What's your excuse for someone who buys ivory and exotic wood bookcases, collects works by unknown or terrible authors, and sits there yawning among thousands of books? He likes their spines and titles more than what's actually inside them. You'll find this in the homes of the laziest people — shelves packed floor to ceiling with every orator and historian ever written. These days a library is as essential to a house as hot and cold running water. I'd forgive them if they were genuinely obsessed with literature. But they're not. These expensive works of genius, with all their beautiful illustrations, are just bought for decoration and to fill wall space.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText:
Suppose, however, that your life has become full of trouble, and
that without knowing what you were doing you have fallen into some
snare which either public or private Fortune has set for you, and
that you can neither untie it nor break it: then remember that
fettered men suffer much at first from the burdens and clogs upon
their legs: afterwards, when they have made up their minds not to
fret themselves about them, but to endure them, necessity teaches
them to bear them bravely, and habit to bear them easily. In every
station of life you will find amusements, relaxations, and enjoyments;
that is, provided you be willing to make light of evils rather than
to hate them. Knowing to what sorrows we were born, there is nothing
for which Nature more deserves our thanks than for having invented
habit as an alleviation of misfortune, which soon accustoms us to
the severest evils. No one could hold out against misfortune if it
permanently exercised the same force as at its first onset.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish:
But suppose your life has become a mess. You've stumbled into some trap — maybe set by politics or personal bad luck — and you can't escape. You can't untangle it or break free. Remember how prisoners suffer terribly at first from their chains. The weight hurts. The metal cuts. But once they stop fighting and accept their situation, something changes. Necessity teaches them to bear it with courage. Habit makes it feel lighter.

You can find moments of joy and peace in any situation — if you choose to take troubles lightly instead of hating them. We were born knowing we'd face sorrow. Nothing shows nature's kindness more than this: she gave us the ability to get used to things. Habit softens even the worst disasters. If misfortune kept hitting us with the same brutal force as that first blow, no one could survive it.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText:
We are
