all chained to Fortune: some men’s chain is loose and made of gold,
that of others is tight and of meaner metal: but what difference
does this make? we are all included in the same captivity, and even
those who have bound us are bound themselves, unless you think that
a chain on the left side is lighter to bear: one man may be bound
by public office, another by wealth: some have to bear the
weight of illustrious, some of humble birth: some are subject to
the commands of others, some only to their own: some are kept in
one place by being banished thither, others by being elected to the
priesthood. All life is slavery: let each man therefore reconcile
himself to his lot, complain of it as little as possible, and lay
hold of whatever good lies within his reach. No condition can be
so wretched that an impartial mind can find no compensations in it.
Small sites, if ingeniously divided, may be made use of for many
different purposes, and arrangement will render ever so narrow a
room habitable.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: We are all chained to Fortune. Some people wear loose chains made of gold. Others wear tight chains made of cheaper metal. But what's the difference? We're all prisoners together. Even the people who bound us are bound themselves. Do you think a chain on your left hand is easier to carry? One person may be chained by public office, another by wealth. Some must bear the weight of noble birth, others of humble origins. Some obey other people's commands, some only their own. Some are stuck in one place by exile, others by being chosen as priests. All life is slavery. So each person should accept their situation. Complain as little as possible. Grab whatever good you can reach. No condition is so miserable that a fair mind can't find some compensation in it.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText:
Call good sense to your aid against difficulties:
it is possible to soften what is harsh, to widen what is too narrow,
and to make heavy burdens press less severely upon one who bears
them skilfully. Moreover, we ought not to allow our desires to
wander far afield, but we must make them confine themselves to our
immediate neighbourhood, since they will not endure to be altogether
locked up. We must leave alone things which either cannot come to
pass or can only be effected with difficulty, and follow after such
things as are near at hand and within reach of our hopes, always
remembering that all things are equally unimportant, and that though
they have a different outward appearance, they are all alike empty
within. Neither let us envy those who are in high places: the heights
which look lofty to us are steep and rugged. Again, those whom
unkind fate has placed in critical situations will be safer if they
show as little pride in their proud position as may be, and do all
they are able to bring down their fortunes to the level of other
men’s.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: Small spaces can serve many purposes if you divide them cleverly. Good planning can make even the narrowest room livable. Use common sense to handle problems. You can soften what's harsh, expand what's cramped, and make heavy burdens lighter if you carry them skillfully. Don't let your desires roam too far. Keep them focused on what's nearby, since they won't tolerate being completely shut down. Leave alone things that can't happen or are very difficult to achieve. Go after things that are close and within reach of your hopes. Always remember that all things are equally unimportant. They may look different on the outside, but inside they're all equally empty.

peace-of-mind_section-10.originalText:
There are many who must needs cling to their high pinnacle
of power, because they cannot descend from it save by falling
headlong: yet they assure us that their greatest burden is being
obliged to be burdensome to others, and that they are nailed to
their lofty post rather than raised to it: let them then, by
dispensing justice, clemency, and kindness with an open and liberal
hand, provide themselves with assistance to break their fall, and
looking forward to this maintain their position more hopefully. Yet
nothing sets us free from these alternations of hope and fear so
well as always fixing some limit to our successes, and not allowing
Fortune to choose when to stop our career, but to halt of our own
accord long before we apparently need do so. By acting thus certain
desires will rouse up our spirits, and yet being confined within
bounds, will not lead us to embark on vast and vague enterprises.
peace-of-mind_section-10.plainEnglish: Don't envy people in high positions. Those heights that look impressive to us are steep and dangerous. And those whom cruel fate has put in risky situations will be safer if they show less pride in their position. They should do everything they can to bring their fortunes down to everyone else's level. Many people have to cling to their high places of power because they can't come down except by falling hard. Yet they tell us their biggest burden is being forced to burden others. They say they're nailed to their high post rather than lifted up to it. So let them hand out justice, mercy, and kindness freely and generously. This will give them help to cushion their fall. Looking ahead to this will help them hold their position with more hope. But nothing frees us from these swings between hope and fear like setting some limit on our success. Don't let Fortune choose when to stop your career. Stop on your own, long before you apparently need to. If you do this, certain desires will still stir your spirit. But since they're kept within bounds, they won't lead you into huge and uncertain ventures.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
These remarks of mine apply only to imperfect, commonplace, and
unsound natures, not to the wise man, who needs not to walk with
timid and cautious gait: for he has such confidence in himself that
he does not hesitate to go directly in the teeth of Fortune, and
never will give way to her. Nor indeed has he any reason for fearing
her, for he counts not only chattels, property, and high office,
but even his body, his eyes, his hands, and everything whose use
makes life dearer to us, nay, even his very self, to be things whose
possession is uncertain; he lives as though he had borrowed them,
and is ready to return them cheerfully whenever they are claimed.
Yet he does not hold himself cheap, because he knows that he is not
his own, but performs all his duties as carefully and prudently as
a pious and scrupulous man would take care of property left in his
charge as trustee. When he is bidden to give them up, he will not
complain of Fortune, but will say, “I thank you for what I have had
possession of: I have managed your property so as largely to increase
it, but since you order me, I give it back to you and return it
willingly and thankfully.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: What I've said so far only applies to people who are flawed, ordinary, and unwise. It doesn't apply to the wise person, who doesn't need to walk around scared and careful. He has so much confidence in himself that he doesn't hesitate to face Fortune head-on. He will never back down from her. He has no reason to fear her either. He knows that not just his possessions, property, and high positions are uncertain — but even his body, his eyes, his hands, and everything that makes life precious to him. Even his very self. He lives as if he had borrowed all these things, and he's ready to give them back cheerfully whenever they're asked for.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
If you still wish me to own anything of
yours, I will keep it for you: if you have other views, I restore
into your hands and make restitution of all my wrought and coined
silver, my house and my household. Should Nature recall what
she previously entrusted us with, let us say to her also: ‘Take
back my spirit, which is better than when you gave it me: I do not
shuffle or hang back. Of my own free will I am ready to return what
you gave me before I could think: take me away,’” What hardship can
there be in returning to the place from whence one came? a man
cannot live well if he knows not how to die well. We must, therefore,
take away from this commodity its original value, and count the
breath of life as a cheap matter. “We dislike gladiators,” says
Cicero, “if they are eager to save their lives by any means whatever:
but we look favourably upon them if they are openly reckless of
them,” You may be sure that the same thing occurs with us: we often
die because we are afraid of death.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: But he doesn't think little of himself. He knows he's not really his own person. He handles all his duties carefully and wisely, like a good and honest person taking care of property that belongs to someone else. When he's told to give these things up, he won't complain about bad luck. Instead he'll say, "Thank you for letting me use these things. I managed your property well and made it grow. But since you're asking for it back, I return it willingly and gratefully. If you still want me to hold onto anything of yours, I'll keep it safe. If you've changed your mind, I give back everything — my silver coins, my house, my servants." And if Nature wants back what she first gave us, let's say to her too: "Take back my soul. It's better now than when you gave it to me. I'm not hesitating or holding back. I'm ready to return what you gave me before I could even think about it. Take me away."

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
Fortune, which regards our lives
as a show in the arena for her own enjoyment, says, “Why should I
spare you, base and cowardly creature that you are? you will be
pierced and hacked with all the more wounds because you know not
how to offer your throat to the knife: whereas you, who receive the
stroke without drawing away your neck or putting up your hands to
stop it, shall both live longer and die more quickly,” He who fears
death will never act as becomes a living man: but he who knows that
this fate was laid upon him as soon as he was conceived will live
according to it, and by this strength of mind will gain this further
advantage, that nothing can befal him unexpectedly: for by looking
forward to everything which can happen as though it would happen
to him, he takes the sting out of all evils, which can make no
difference to those who expect it and are prepared to meet it: evil
only comes hard upon those who have lived without giving it a thought
and whose attention has been exclusively directed to happiness.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: What's so hard about going back to where you came from? You can't live well if you don't know how to die well. So we need to strip death of its power to frighten us. We need to see life as something cheap and ordinary. Cicero said, "We hate gladiators who try to save their lives by any means. But we respect the ones who openly throw their lives away." The same thing happens with us. We often die because we're afraid of death. Fortune watches our lives like a show in the arena for her entertainment. She says, "Why should I spare you, you coward? You'll get cut up even worse because you don't know how to offer your throat to the blade. But you — the one who takes the blow without pulling back or throwing up your hands — you'll live longer and die faster."

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
Disease, captivity, disaster, conflagration, are none of them
unexpected: I always knew with what disorderly company Nature
had associated me. The dead have often been wailed for in my
neighbourhood: the torch and taper have often been borne past my
door before the bier of one who has died before his time: the crash
of falling buildings has often resounded by my side: night has
snatched away many of those with whom I have become intimate in the
forum, the Senate-house, and in society, and has sundered the hands
which were joined in friendship: ought I to be surprised if the
dangers which have always been circling around me at last assail
me? How large a part of mankind never think of storms when about
to set sail? I shall never be ashamed to quote a good saying because
it comes from a bad author. Publilius, who was a more powerful
writer than any of our other playwrights, whether comic or tragic,
whenever he chose to rise above farcical absurdities and speeches
addressed to the gallery, among many other verses too noble even
for tragedy, let alone for comedy, has this one:—
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: Someone who fears death will never live like they're truly alive. But someone who knows that death was assigned to them from the moment they were born will live according to that fact. This mental strength gives them another advantage: nothing can catch them off guard. By expecting everything that could happen as if it will happen to them, they remove the pain from all troubles. Problems can't hurt people who see them coming and are ready for them. Trouble only hits hard when it strikes people who never thought about it — people who only focused on being happy.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText: “What one hath suffered may befall us all.”
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: Disease, imprisonment, disaster, fire — none of these should surprise me. I've always known what messy company nature has given me as fellow humans. I've often heard people weeping for the dead in my neighborhood. I've often seen torches and candles carried past my door, ahead of someone who died too young. I've heard buildings collapse nearby many times. Death has taken away many people I knew well from the forum, the Senate, and social gatherings. It has broken apart hands that were joined in friendship. Should I really be surprised when the dangers that have always circled around me finally come for me too?

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
If a man takes this into his inmost heart and looks upon all the
misfortunes of other men, of which there is always a great plenty,
in this spirit, remembering that there is nothing to prevent their
coming upon him also, he will arm himself against them long before
they attack him. It is too late to school the mind to endurance of
peril after peril has come. “I did not think this would happen,”
and “Would you ever have believed that this would have happened?”
say you. But why should it not? Where are the riches after which
want, hunger, and beggary do not follow? what office is there whose
purple robe, augur’s staff, and patrician reins have not as their
accompaniment rags and banishment, the brand of infamy, a thousand
disgraces, and utter reprobation? what kingdom is there for which
ruin, trampling under foot, a tyrant and a butcher are not
ready at hand? nor are these matters divided by long periods of
time, but there is but the space of an hour between sitting on the
throne ourselves and clasping the knees of some one else as suppliants.
Know then that every station of life is transitory, and that what
has ever happened to anybody may happen to you also.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish:
How many people never think about storms when they're about to set sail? I'm not ashamed to quote a good line just because it comes from a bad writer. Publilius was a better writer than any of our other playwrights, whether they wrote comedies or tragedies. When he stopped writing silly jokes and crowd-pleasing speeches, he came up with lines too good even for serious drama. Here's one of them:

"What one person has suffered can happen to any of us."

If you really take this to heart and look at all the terrible things that happen to other people — and there are plenty of them — while remembering that nothing stops these same things from happening to you, you'll prepare yourself for trouble long before it arrives.

peace-of-mind_section-11.originalText:
You are wealthy:
are you wealthier than Pompeius?[6] Yet when Gaius,[7] his old
relative and new host, opened Caesar’s house to him in order that
he might close his own, he lacked both bread and water: though he
owned so many rivers which both rose and discharged themselves
within his dominions, yet he had to beg for drops of water: he
perished of hunger and thirst in the palace of his relative, while
his heir was contracting for a public funeral for one who was in
want of food. You have filled public offices: were they either as
important, as unlooked for, or as all-embracing as those of Sejanus?
Yet on the day on which the Senate disgraced him, the people tore
him to pieces: the executioner[8] could find no part left large
enough to drag to the Tiber, of one upon whom gods and men had
showered all that could be given to man. You are a king: I will not
bid you go to Croesus for an example, he who while yet alive saw
his funeral pile both lighted and extinguished, being made to outlive
not only his kingdom but even his own death, nor to Jugurtha, whom
the people of Rome beheld as a captive within the year in which
they had feared him. We have seen Ptolemaeus King of Africa, and
Mithridates King of Armenia, under the charge of Gaius’s[9] guards:
the former was sent into exile, the latter chose it in order to
make his exile more honourable. Among such continual topsy-turvy
changes, unless you expect that whatever can happen will happen to
you, you give adversity power against you, a power which can be
destroyed by any one who looks at it beforehand.
peace-of-mind_section-11.plainEnglish: It's too late to train your mind for danger once the danger has already arrived. You say, "I didn't think this would happen," and "Who could have believed this would happen?" But why shouldn't it happen? What riches exist that aren't followed by poverty, hunger, and begging? What political office comes with its purple robes, ceremonial staff, and noble privileges without also bringing the possibility of rags, exile, public shame, a thousand humiliations, and total disgrace? What kingdom exists without ruin, conquest, tyrants, and executioners waiting in the wings? These reversals don't take centuries to unfold. There's only an hour's difference between sitting on a throne yourself and begging on your knees before someone else.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText:
The next point to these will be to take care that we do not
labour for what is vain, or labour in vain: that is to say, neither
to desire what we are not able to obtain, nor yet, having obtained
our desire too late, and after much toil to discover the folly of
our wishes: in other words, that our labour may not be without
result, and that the result may not be unworthy of our labour: for
as a rule sadness arises from one of these two things, either from
want of success or from being ashamed of having succeeded. We must
limit the running to and fro which most men practise, rambling about
houses, theatres, and market-places. They mind other men’s business,
and always seem as though they themselves had something to do. If
you ask one of them as he comes out of his own door, “Whither are
you going?” he will answer, “By Hercules, I do not know: but I shall
see some people and do something.” They wander purposelessly seeking
for something to do, and do, not what they have made up their minds
to do, but what has casually fallen in their way. They move uselessly
and without any plan, just like ants crawling over bushes, which
creep up to the top and then down to the bottom again without gaining
anything. Many men spend their lives in exactly the same fashion,
which one may call a state of restless indolence.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: The next thing to watch out for is that we don't work for worthless things, or work uselessly. Don't chase things you can't get. And don't work so hard for something that by the time you finally get it, you realize how foolish you were to want it in the first place. Make sure your work leads to something worthwhile. And make sure what you achieve is actually worth the effort you put in. Most sadness comes from one of two places: either you fail to get what you want, or you succeed and then feel ashamed of what you wanted.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText:
You would pity
some of them when you see them running as if their house was on
fire: they actually jostle all whom they meet, and hurry along
themselves and others with them, though all the while they are going
to salute some one who will not return their greeting, or to attend
the funeral of some one whom they did not know: they are going to
hear the verdict on one who often goes to law, or to see the
wedding of one who often gets married: they will follow a man’s
litter, and in some places will even carry it: afterwards returning
home weary with idleness, they swear that they themselves do not
know why they went out, or where they have been, and on the following
day they will wander through the same round again.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: We need to stop the endless running around that most people do. They wander from house to house, from theaters to markets. They stick their noses into everyone else's business and always act like they have something important to do. If you catch one of them leaving his house and ask "Where are you going?" he'll say, "God, I don't know. But I'll see some people and do something." They drift around aimlessly looking for something to do. And they don't do what they planned — they do whatever happens to cross their path. They move without purpose or plan, like ants crawling over bushes. The ants climb to the top, then back down to the bottom, getting nowhere. Many people live exactly this way. You could call it restless laziness.

peace-of-mind_section-12.originalText:
Let all your
work, therefore, have some purpose, and keep some object in view:
these restless people are not made restless by labour, but are
driven out of their minds by mistaken ideas: for even they do not
put themselves in motion without any hope: they are excited by the
outward appearance of something, and their crazy mind cannot see
its futility. In the same way every one of those who walk out to
swell the crowd in the streets, is led round the city by worthless
and empty reasons; the dawn drives him forth, although he has nothing
to do, and after he has pushed his way into many men’s doors, and
saluted their nomenclators one after the other, and been turned
away from many others, he finds that the most difficult person of
all to find at home is himself. From this evil habit comes that
worst of all vices, talebearing and prying into public and private
secrets, and the knowledge of many things which it is neither safe
to tell nor safe to listen to.
peace-of-mind_section-12.plainEnglish: You would feel sorry for some people when you see them rushing around like their house is on fire. They bump into everyone they meet and drag themselves and others along with them. But where are they going? To greet someone who won't greet them back. To attend a funeral for someone they never knew. To hear the verdict for someone who's always in court. To watch the wedding of someone who gets married all the time. They'll follow some important person's sedan chair, and sometimes even help carry it. Then they come home exhausted from all this pointless activity. They swear they don't even know why they went out or where they've been. And the next day? They'll do the exact same thing all over again.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Moreover, we ought to cultivate an easy temper, and not become over fond of the lot which fate has assigned to us, but transfer ourselves to whatever other condition chance may lead us to, and fear no alteration, either in our purposes or our position in life, provided that we do not become subject to caprice, which of all vices is the most hostile to repose: for obstinacy, from which Fortune often wrings some concession, must needs be anxious and unhappy, but caprice, which can never restrain itself, must be more so. Both of these qualities, both that of altering nothing, and that of being dissatisfied with everything, are energies to repose. The mind ought in all cases to be called away from the contemplation of external things to that of itself: let it confide in itself, rejoice in itself, admire its own works; avoid as far as may be those of others, and devote itself to itself; let it not feel losses, and put a good construction even upon misfortunes.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: We should also stay flexible and not get too attached to whatever life fate has given us. When chance leads us somewhere new, we should go with it. Don't fear changes to your plans or your place in life. Just don't let yourself become fickle — that's the worst enemy of peace of mind. Stubbornness makes you anxious and miserable, especially when Fortune forces you to give in anyway. But fickleness is even worse, since it can never settle down. Both extremes — never changing anything and being unhappy with everything — are enemies of inner peace. Your mind should turn away from focusing on outside things and focus on itself instead. Let it trust itself, enjoy itself, and admire its own work. Avoid other people's affairs as much as possible and devote yourself to yourself. Don't feel every loss so deeply, and try to see even misfortunes in a good light.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Zeno, the chief of our school, when he heard the news of a shipwreck, in which all his property had been lost, remarked, "Fortune bids me follow philosophy in lighter marching order." A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death, and even with want of burial. "You are able to please yourself," he answered, "my half pint of blood is in your power: for, as for burial, what a fool you must be if you suppose that I care whether I rot above ground or under it."
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Zeno, the founder of our school, heard that his ship had sunk and all his wealth was gone. He said, "Fortune is telling me to pursue philosophy with less baggage." A tyrant threatened Theodorus with death and told him he wouldn't even get a proper burial. Theodorus replied, "Do whatever makes you happy. You can spill my blood if you want. But burial? You'd have to be an idiot to think I care whether I rot above ground or below it."

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Julius Kanus, a man of peculiar greatness, whom even the fact of his having been born in this century does not prevent our admiring, had a long dispute with Gaius, and when as he was going away that Phalaris of a man said to him, "That you may not delude yourself with any foolish hopes, I have ordered you to be executed," he answered, "I thank you, most excellent prince." I am not sure what he meant: for many ways of explaining his conduct occur to me. Did he wish to be reproachful, and to show him how great his cruelty must be if death became a kindness? or did he upbraid him with his accustomed insanity? for even those whose children were put to death, and whose goods were confiscated, used to thank him: or was it that he willingly received death, regarding it as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a magnanimous answer. Some one may say, "After this Gaius might have let him live." Kanus had no fear of this: the good faith with which Gaius carried out such orders as these was well known.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Julius Kanus was an extraordinary man. Even being born in our wicked century doesn't stop us from admiring him. He had a long argument with Gaius. As Kanus was leaving, that tyrant said to him, "Don't fool yourself with false hopes. I've ordered your execution." Kanus replied, "Thank you, most excellent prince." I'm not sure what he meant. Several explanations come to mind. Was he being sarcastic to show Gaius how cruel he was — making death seem like a gift? Was he mocking Gaius's usual madness? After all, even people whose children were killed and property seized used to thank him. Or did Kanus genuinely welcome death as freedom? Whatever he meant, it was a brave answer. Someone might say, "After this, Gaius could have spared him." Kanus wasn't worried about that. Everyone knew Gaius always followed through on execution orders.

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Will you believe that he passed the ten intervening days before his execution without the slightest despondency? it is marvellous how that man spoke and acted, and how peaceful he was. He was playing at draughts when the centurion in charge of a number of those who where going to be executed bade him join them: on the summons he counted his men and said to his companion, "Mind you do not tell a lie after my death, and say that you won;" then, turning to the centurion, he said "You will bear me witness that I am one man ahead of him." Do you think that Kanus played upon that draught-board? nay, he played with it. His friends were sad at being about to lose so great a man: "Why," asked he, "are you sorrowful? you are enquiring whether our souls are immortal, but I shall presently know."
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Can you believe this man spent his last ten days without any despair? It's amazing how he spoke and acted. How calm he was. He was playing checkers when the centurion came to collect the men scheduled for execution. When called, he counted his pieces and told his opponent, "Don't lie after I'm dead and claim you were winning." Then he turned to the centurion and said, "You can confirm I'm ahead by one piece." Do you think Kanus was just playing a game? No — he was making a point about life itself. His friends were sad they were losing such a great man. "Why are you upset?" he asked. "You wonder if our souls live on after death. Well, I'm about to find out."

peace-of-mind_section-14.originalText: Nor did he up to the very end cease his search after truth, and raised arguments upon the subject of his own death. His own teacher of philosophy accompanied him, and they were not far from the hill on which the daily sacrifice to Caesar our god was offered, when he said, "What are you thinking of now, Kanus? or what are your ideas?" "I have decided," answered Kanus, "at that most swiftly-passing moment of all to watch whether the spirit will be conscious of the act of leaving the body." He promised, too, that if he made any discoveries, he would come round to his friends and tell them what the condition of the souls of the departed might be. Here was peace in the very midst of the storm: here was a soul worthy of eternal life, which used its own fate as a proof of truth, which when at the last step of life experimented upon his fleeting breath, and did not merely continue to learn until he died, but learned something even from death itself. No man has carried the life of a philosopher further. I will not hastily leave the subject of a great man, and one who deserves to be spoken of with respect: I will hand thee down to all posterity, thou most noble heart, chief among the many victims of Gaius.
peace-of-mind_section-14.plainEnglish: Right up until the end, he never stopped searching for truth. He even debated questions about his own death. His philosophy teacher walked with him, and they were close to the hill where the daily sacrifice to Caesar our god was made. His teacher asked, "What are you thinking about right now, Kanus? What's on your mind?" "I've decided," Kanus answered, "to watch very carefully in that quickest moment of all — to see if my spirit will know it's leaving my body." He even promised that if he learned anything, he would visit his friends and tell them what it's like for souls after death. Here was calm right in the middle of a storm. Here was a soul that deserved eternal life — one that used his own fate to test the truth. At life's final step, he experimented with his own dying breath. He didn't just keep learning until he died. He learned something even from death itself. No one has taken the philosopher's life further than this. I won't rush past this great man who deserves our respect. I will pass you down to all future generations, you most noble heart, the greatest among all of Gaius's many victims.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: Yet we gain nothing by getting rid of all personal causes of sadness, for sometimes we are possessed by hatred of the human race. When you reflect how rare simplicity is, how unknown innocence, how seldom faith is kept, unless it be to our advantage, when you remember such numbers of successful crimes, so many equally hateful losses and gains of lust, and ambition so impatient even of its own natural limits that it is willing to purchase distinction by baseness, the mind seems as it were cast into darkness, and shadows rise before it as though the virtues were all overthrown and we were no longer allowed to hope to possess them or benefited by their possession.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: But getting rid of personal reasons for sadness doesn't solve everything. Sometimes we're overwhelmed by hatred for the entire human race. You see how rare honesty is, how unknown innocence has become, how rarely people keep their word unless it benefits them. You remember all those successful crimes, all the disgusting gains from lust and ambition. You see ambition so desperate that it will buy fame with shameful acts. When you think about all this, your mind feels like it's been plunged into darkness. Shadows rise up as if all the virtues have been destroyed and we can no longer hope to have them or gain anything from them.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: We ought therefore to bring ourselves into such a state of mind that all the vices of the vulgar may not appear hateful to us, but merely ridiculous, and we should imitate Democritus rather than Heraclitus. The latter of these, whenever be appeared in public, used to weep, the former to laugh: the one thought all human doings to be follies, the other thought them to be miseries. We must take a higher view of all things, and bear with them more easily: it better becomes a man to scoff at life than to lament over it. Add to this that he who laughs at the human race deserves better of it than he who mourns for it, for the former leaves it some good hopes of improvement, while the latter stupidly weeps over what he has given up all hopes of mending. He who after surveying the universe cannot control his laughter shows, too, a greater mind than he who cannot restrain his tears, because his mind is only affected in the slightest possible degree, and he does not think that any part of all this apparatus is either important, or serious, or unhappy.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: We should train our minds to see the common faults of ordinary people as funny rather than disgusting. We should be like Democritus, not Heraclitus. When Heraclitus went out in public, he would weep. When Democritus went out, he would laugh. One saw human behavior as tragic. The other saw it as foolish. We need to take a higher view of everything and put up with it more easily. It's better for a person to laugh at life than to cry over it. Here's another reason: someone who laughs at humanity serves it better than someone who mourns for it. Laughter suggests there's still hope for improvement. Mourning stupidly gives up on any chance of fixing things. When someone looks at the whole universe and can't help but laugh, they show a greater mind than someone who can't stop their tears. Their mind is barely affected at all. They don't think any part of this whole show is important, serious, or tragic.

peace-of-mind_section-15.originalText: As for the several causes which render us happy or sorrowful, let every one describe them for himself, and learn the truth of Bion's saying, "That all the doings of men were very like what he began with, and that there is nothing in their lives which is more holy or decent than their conception." Yet it is better to accept public morals and human vices calmly without bursting into either laughter or tears; for to be hurt by the sufferings of others is to be for ever miserable, while to enjoy the sufferings of others is an inhuman pleasure, just as it is a useless piece of humanity to weep and pull a long face because some one is burying his son. In one's own misfortunes, also, one ought so to conduct oneself as to bestow upon them just as much sorrow as reason, not as much as custom requires: for many shed tears in order to show them, and whenever no one is looking at them their eyes are dry, but they think it disgraceful not to weep when every one does so. So deeply has this evil of being guided by the opinion of others taken root in us, that even grief, the simplest of all emotions, begins to be counterfeited.
peace-of-mind_section-15.plainEnglish: Everyone has their own reasons for being happy or sad. Each person should think about what those reasons are for themselves. This will help them understand what Bion meant when he said that everything people do is just like how they started out in life — there's nothing more pure or proper in their whole existence than their very beginning. Still, it's better to accept society's flaws and human weaknesses calmly. Don't burst into laughter or tears over them. Getting upset by other people's suffering will make you miserable forever. Enjoying other people's suffering is cruel. And it's pointless to weep and make a big show of sadness just because someone is burying their child.

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText:
There comes now a part of our subject which is wont with good
cause to make one sad and anxious: I mean when good men come to bad
ends; when Socrates is forced to die in prison, Rutilius to live
in exile, Pompeius and Cicero to offer their necks to the swords
of their own followers, when the great Cato, that living image of
virtue, falls upon his sword and rips up both himself and the
republic, one cannot help being grieved that Fortune should bestow
her gifts so unjustly: what, too, can a good man hope to obtain
when he sees the best of men meeting with the worst fates. Well,
but see how each of them endured his fate, and if they endured it
bravely, long in your heart for courage as great as theirs; if they
died in a womanish and cowardly manner, nothing was lost: either
they deserved that you should admire their courage, or else they
did not deserve that you should wish to imitate their cowardice:
for what can be more shameful than that the greatest men should die
so bravely as to make people cowards.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: Now we reach a part of our topic that naturally makes anyone feel sad and worried. I mean when good men come to terrible ends. Socrates was forced to die in prison. Rutilius had to live in exile. Pompey and Cicero had to offer their necks to the swords of their own followers. The great Cato — that living image of virtue — fell on his sword and destroyed both himself and the republic. When you see things like this, you can't help feeling upset that Fortune hands out her rewards so unfairly. What hope can a good man have when he sees the best people meeting the worst fates?

peace-of-mind_section-16.originalText:
Let us praise one who deserves
such constant praises, and say, “The braver you are the happier you
are! You have escaped from all accidents, jealousies, diseases: you
have escaped from prison: the gods have not thought you worthy of
ill-fortune, but have thought that fortune no longer deserved to
have any power over you”: but when any one shrinks back in the hour
of death and looks longingly at life, we must lay hands upon him.
I will never weep for a man who dies cheerfully, nor for one who
dies weeping: the former wipes away my tears, the latter by his
tears makes himself unworthy that any should be shed for him. Shall
I weep for Hercules because he was burned alive, or for Regulus
because he was pierced by so many nails, or for Cato because he
tore open his wounds a second time? All these men discovered how
at the cost of a small portion of time they might obtain immortality,
and by their deaths gained eternal life.
peace-of-mind_section-16.plainEnglish: But look at how each of them faced their fate. If they endured it bravely, then long for courage like theirs. If they died in a weak and cowardly way, nothing was lost. Either they earned your admiration for their courage, or they didn't deserve to have you copy their cowardice. What could be more shameful than great men dying so bravely that it makes other people into cowards?

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: It also proves a fertile source of troubles if you take pains to conceal your feelings and never show yourself to any one undisguised, but, as many men do, live an artificial life, in order to impose upon others: for the constant watching of himself becomes a torment to a man, and he dreads being caught doing something at variance with his usual habits, and, indeed, we never can be at our ease if we imagine that every one who looks at us is weighing our real value: for many things occur which strip people of their disguise, however reluctantly they may part with it, and even if all this trouble about oneself is successful, still life is neither happy nor safe when one always has to wear a mask. But what pleasure there is in that honest straight-forwardness which is its own ornament, and which conceals no part of its character! Yet even this life, which hides nothing from any one runs some risk of being despised; for there are people who disdain whatever they come close to: but there is no danger of virtue's becoming contemptible when she is brought near our eyes, and it is better to be scorned for one's simplicity than to bear the burden of unceasing hypocrisy. Still, we must observe moderation in this matter, for there is a great difference between living simply and living slovenly.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: It causes endless trouble when you try to hide your true feelings and never let anyone see the real you. Many people live fake lives to impress others. But constantly watching yourself becomes torture. You're always afraid someone will catch you acting differently than usual. We can never relax when we think everyone is judging our worth. Many things will eventually strip away your disguise, no matter how hard you try to keep it. And even if you succeed in fooling everyone, life is neither happy nor safe when you always have to wear a mask. How much better it is to be honest and straightforward! This kind of life is its own decoration and hides nothing about who you are. Of course, this open life does risk being looked down on — some people despise anything they get close to. But virtue never becomes contemptible when people see it up close. It's better to be scorned for being simple than to carry the heavy burden of constant pretending.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Moreover, we ought to retire a great deal into ourselves: for association with persons unlike ourselves upsets all that we had arranged, rouses the passions which were at rest, and rubs into a sore any weak or imperfectly healed place in our minds. Nevertheless we ought to mix up these two things, and to pass our lives alternately in solitude and among throngs of people; for the former will make us long for the society of mankind, the latter for that of ourselves, and the one will counteract the other: solitude will cure us when we are sick of crowds, and crowds will cure us when we are sick of solitude.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: Still, we need to find the right balance here. There's a big difference between living simply and living like a slob. We should spend plenty of time alone with ourselves. Being around people who are different from us messes up our plans, stirs up emotions we had calmed down, and reopens wounds that hadn't fully healed in our minds. But we need to mix these two things together. We should alternate between being alone and being with crowds of people. Solitude will make us crave human company, and crowds will make us crave solitude. Each one balances out the other. Solitude heals us when we're sick of crowds, and crowds heal us when we're sick of being alone.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Neither ought we always to keep the mind strained to the same pitch, but it ought sometimes to be relaxed by amusement. Socrates did not blush to play with little boys, Cato used to refresh his mind with wine after he had wearied it with application to affairs of state, and Scipio would move his triumphal and soldierly limbs to the sound of music, not with a feeble and halting gait, as is the fashion now-a-days, when we sway in our very walk with more than womanly weakness, but dancing as men were wont in the days of old on sportive and festal occasions, with manly bounds, thinking it no harm to be seen so doing even by their enemies. Men's minds ought to have relaxation: they rise up better and more vigorous after rest. We must not force crops from rich fields, for an unbroken course of heavy crops will soon exhaust their fertility, and so also the liveliness of our minds will be destroyed by unceasing labour, but they will recover their strength after a short period of rest and relief: for continuous toil produces a sort of numbness and sluggishness.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: We shouldn't keep our minds constantly under pressure. Sometimes we need to relax with some fun. Socrates wasn't embarrassed to play with little children. Cato would refresh his mind with wine after wearing himself out with government business. Scipio would dance to music with his battle-tested body — not with the weak, shuffling steps we see today, where people can barely walk without swaying like they're about to collapse. He danced the way men used to at parties and festivals, with strong, manly movements. He didn't care if even his enemies saw him doing it. Our minds need breaks. They bounce back stronger and more energetic after rest. You wouldn't force crops from rich soil year after year — constant heavy harvesting would drain the land completely. The same thing happens to our minds. Non-stop work kills their sharpness. But they recover their strength after a short rest. Continuous labor creates a kind of mental numbness and sluggishness.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: Men would not be so eager for this, if play and amusement did not possess natural attractions for them, although constant indulgence in them takes away all gravity and all strength from the mind: for sleep, also, is necessary for our refreshment, yet if you prolong it for days and nights together it will become death. There is a great difference between slackening your hold of a thing and letting it go. The founders of our laws appointed festivals, in order that men might be publicly encouraged to be cheerful, and they thought it necessary to vary our labours with amusements, and, as I said before, some great men have been wont to give themselves a certain number of holidays in every month, and some divided every day into play-time and work-time. Thus, I remember that great orator Asinius Pollio would not attend to any business after the tenth hour: he would not even read letters after that time for fear some new trouble should arise, but in those two hours used to get rid of the weariness which he had contracted during the whole day. Some rest in the middle of the day, and reserve some light occupation for the afternoon. Our ancestors, too, forbade any new motion to be made in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watches, and those who have just returned from active service are allowed to sleep the whole night undisturbed.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: People wouldn't crave entertainment so much if fun and games didn't appeal to us naturally. But too much of them drains all seriousness and strength from your mind. Sleep is necessary to refresh us, but if you sleep for days on end, it becomes death. There's a big difference between loosening your grip on something and completely letting go. The founders of our laws created festivals so people would be publicly encouraged to be cheerful. They thought it was necessary to break up our work with amusement. As I said before, some great men gave themselves a certain number of holidays each month. Others divided every day into playtime and work time. I remember that great speaker Asinius Pollio wouldn't handle any business after the tenth hour. He wouldn't even read letters after that time, afraid some new trouble would come up. He used those two hours to shake off the weariness he'd built up during the whole day. Some people rest in the middle of the day and save light tasks for the afternoon. Our ancestors also forbade any new business in the Senate after the tenth hour. Soldiers divide their watches, and those who've just returned from active duty get to sleep through the whole night undisturbed.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: If we believe the Greek poet, "it is sometimes pleasant to be mad"; again, Plato always knocked in vain at the door of poetry when he was sober; or, if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever been without a touch of insanity. The mind cannot use lofty language, above that of the common herd, unless it be excited. When it has spurned aside the commonplace environments of custom, and rises sublime, instinct with sacred fire, then alone can it chant a song too grand for mortal lips: as long as it continues to dwell within itself it cannot rise to any pitch of splendour: it must break away from the beaten track, and lash itself to frenzy, till it gnaws the curb and rushes away bearing up its rider to heights whither it would fear to climb when alone.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: If we believe the Greek poet, "it's sometimes pleasant to be mad." Plato could never write great poetry when he was sober. And if we trust Aristotle, no great genius has ever existed without a touch of insanity. The mind can't use grand language — the kind that rises above ordinary speech — unless it gets excited. When it breaks free from everyday customs and rises up, filled with sacred fire, only then can it sing a song too magnificent for human lips. As long as the mind stays calm and normal, it can't reach any heights of brilliance. It must break away from the safe, well-worn path. It must drive itself into a frenzy, bite at the bit, and rush forward, carrying its rider to heights it would be too scared to climb alone.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: I've now told you, my dear Serenus, what can protect peace of mind, what can bring it back when we lose it, and what can stop the hidden flaws that slowly destroy it. But know this: none of these methods is strong enough to help us keep such a slippery blessing unless we watch our wavering mind with intense and constant care.

peace-of-mind_section-17.originalText: We must humour our minds and grant them rest from time to time, which acts upon them like food, and restores their strength. It does good also to take walks out of doors, that our spirits may be raised and refreshed by the open air and fresh breeze: sometimes we gain strength by driving in a carriage, by travel, by change of air, or by social meals and a more generous allowance of wine: at times we ought to drink even to intoxication, not so as to drown, but merely to dip ourselves in wine: for wine washes away troubles and dislodges them from the depths of the mind, and acts as a remedy to sorrow as it does to some diseases. The inventor of wine is called Liber, not from the licence which he gives to our tongues, but because he liberates the mind from the bondage of cares, and emancipates it, animates it, and renders it more daring in all that it attempts. Yet moderation is wholesome both in freedom and in wine. It is believed that Solon and Arcesilaus used to drink deep. Cato is reproached with drunkenness: but whoever casts this in his teeth will find it easier to turn his reproach into a commendation than to prove that Cato did anything wrong: however, we ought not to do it often, for fear the mind should contract evil habits, though it ought sometimes to be forced into frolic and frankness, and to cast off dull sobriety for a while.
peace-of-mind_section-17.plainEnglish: We need to give our minds a break sometimes. Rest restores mental strength just like food restores physical strength. It helps to take walks outside, where the fresh air and breeze can lift our spirits. Sometimes we gain energy from a carriage ride, from travel, from a change of scenery, or from sharing meals with friends and drinking more wine than usual. At times we should even drink to the point of intoxication — not to drown ourselves, but just to dip into wine. Wine washes away our troubles and brings them up from the depths of our minds. It's a remedy for sorrow, just like it is for some diseases. The god who invented wine is called Liber — not because wine loosens our tongues, but because it frees the mind from its chains of worry. It liberates us, energizes us, and makes us bolder in everything we try. But moderation is healthy for both freedom and wine. People say that Solon and Arcesilaus were heavy drinkers. Critics attack Cato for being a drunk. But anyone who throws that accusation at him will find it easier to turn their criticism into praise than to prove Cato ever did anything wrong. Still, we shouldn't do this often, or the mind might pick up bad habits. But sometimes we should force ourselves into playfulness and honesty, and throw off dreary sobriety for a while.

peace-of-mind_section-13.originalText:
It was, I imagine, following out this principle that Democritis
taught that “he who would live at peace must not do much business
either public or private,” referring of course to unnecessary
business: for if there be any necessity for it we ought to transact
not only much but endless business, both public and private; in
cases, however, where no solemn duty invites us to act, we had
better keep ourselves quiet: for he who does many things often puts
himself in Fortune’s power, and it is safest not to tempt her often,
but always to remember her existence, and never to promise oneself
anything on her security. I will set sail unless anything happens
to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my
financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with
them. This is why we say that nothing befals the wise man which he
did not expect—we do not make him exempt from the chances of human
life, but from its mistakes, nor does everything happen to him as
he wished it would, but as he thought it would: now his first thought
was that his purpose might meet with some resistance, and the pain
of disappointed wishes must affect a man’s mind less severely if
he has not been at all events confident of success.
peace-of-mind_section-13.plainEnglish: I think this is what Democritus meant when he said, "Anyone who wants peace of mind shouldn't take on too much business, public or private." Of course, he was talking about unnecessary business. When duty calls, we should handle all the business we need to — even endless amounts of it, both public and private. But when no serious obligation requires us to act, we're better off staying quiet. Someone who does too many things often puts himself at the mercy of Fortune. It's safest not to test her too often. Always remember she exists, and never count on anything as guaranteed. Say instead: "I'll set sail unless something stops me. I'll become praetor if nothing gets in my way. My business deals will work out unless something goes wrong." This is why we say nothing happens to a wise person that he didn't expect. We don't make him immune to life's chances, just to life's mistakes. Everything doesn't happen as he wished, but as he thought it would. His first thought was always that his plans might hit some obstacle. Disappointed hopes hurt much less when you were never completely confident of success.
